data.howToName: How to scale a recipe with eggs
notes: Half an egg is about 1 1/2 tablespoons beaten, or 25 g on a scale.
A large egg is about 50 g out of the shell, about 3 tablespoons beaten.
For cakes, rounding up by half an egg rarely hurts. For cookies, round down.

description: Scale a recipe with eggs without ending up with half an egg. Whole eggs round cleanly, and a beaten egg measured by the spoon solves the awkward halves.

examples.result: The halved cake uses 1 egg, 1 cup flour, 1/2 cup sugar, and 1/2 teaspoon baking powder.
steps: Multiply each amount by 0.5: 2 cups flour become 1 cup, 1 cup sugar becomes 1/2 cup.
Eggs: 2 × 0.5 = 1 egg. Baking powder: 1 teaspoon × 0.5 = 1/2 teaspoon.
examples.title: A cake with 2 eggs, halved to serve 2

examples.result: The scaled muffins use 1 egg plus 1/2 egg, about 1 1/2 tablespoons beaten, and 1 cup flour.
steps: Flour: 2 cups × 0.5 = 1 cup. Sugar: 1 cup × 0.5 = 1/2 cup.
Eggs: 3 × 0.5 = 1 1/2 eggs. Use 1 whole egg plus half a beaten egg, about 1 1/2 tablespoons.
examples.title: 12 muffins with 3 eggs, halved to make 6

faqs.answer: Beat one egg in a small bowl and use half of it, about 1 1/2 tablespoons. On a scale, half a large egg is about 25 g. A large egg is about 50 g out of the shell and about 3 tablespoons beaten, so the maths is easy either way.
faqs.question: How do you measure half an egg?

faqs.answer: Yes, eggs scale up cleanly: 2 become 4, 3 become 6. At larger counts, weighing is easier than counting. A dozen eggs is about 600 g out of the shell.
faqs.question: Do eggs double and triple exactly?

faqs.answer: It depends on the bake. For cakes and quick breads, rounding up by half an egg rarely hurts. For cookies and scones, round down, because extra egg makes them spread and go cakey. When in doubt, beat the egg and measure the half.
faqs.question: Should I round eggs up or down?

faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the most reliable method. Crack the eggs into a bowl, weigh them, and multiply the weight by the factor. A large egg is about 50 g, so 3 eggs is about 150 g, and half of that is 75 g. No fractions, no guessing.
faqs.question: Can I weigh eggs instead of counting them?

faqs.answer: Use the beaten egg method: beat the eggs together and measure out the fraction you need by the tablespoon. A large egg is about 3 tablespoons beaten, so a third of an egg is about 1 tablespoon. For most recipes, rounding to the nearest half egg is close enough.
faqs.question: What if scaling gives me a third of an egg?

faqs.answer: Yes, in cooking. An omelette or a frittata with one egg more or less is still an omelette. In baking, eggs do structural work, so measure them properly. The beaten egg method takes ten seconds and removes the guesswork.
faqs.question: Does an extra egg matter in a savoury dish?

felicityNote: Eggs are the only ingredient that made me buy a scale. Half an egg by the tablespoon works, but half an egg by weight is exact.

parts.meaning: The multiplier for every ingredient. Halving means a factor of 0.5.
The number of servings you want to make.
The number of servings the recipe makes as written.
About 50 g out of the shell, about 3 tablespoons beaten. Half an egg is about 25 g, or 1 1/2 tablespoons.
The amount of one ingredient after scaling.

formula.text: Scale factor = desired servings ÷ original servings. Scaled amount = original amount × scale factor. One large egg is about 50 g, or 3 tablespoons beaten.

howToSteps.name: Find the factor
howToSteps.text: Divide the servings you want by the servings the recipe makes. A recipe for 4 made for 2 has a factor of 0.5.

howToSteps.name: Scale the eggs first
howToSteps.text: Multiply the egg count by the factor. If the result is a whole number, you are done. If it is a fraction, keep going.

howToSteps.name: Beat and measure the fraction
howToSteps.text: Crack one egg into a small bowl, beat it, and measure out the fraction you need. Half an egg is about 1 1/2 tablespoons, or 25 g on a scale.

howToSteps.name: Scale the rest
howToSteps.text: Work down the rest of the ingredient list and multiply each amount by the factor. Flour, sugar, and butter all scale in full.

howToSteps.name: Round with sense
howToSteps.text: For cakes, rounding up by half an egg rarely hurts. For cookies and scones, round down. When in doubt, measure the beaten egg.

lede: Eggs are the one ingredient you cannot simply multiply. A recipe that halves to one and a half eggs needs a beaten egg and a tablespoon, not a guess.

title: How to Scale a Recipe with Eggs in It
tutorial: Eggs are the one ingredient you cannot simply multiply. Flour halves cleanly. Sugar halves cleanly. But a recipe with 3 eggs, halved, calls for 1 1/2 eggs, and there is no such thing as half an egg in the shell. This is the problem that makes people give up on scaling, and the fix takes ten seconds: beat an egg and measure half of it.

A large egg is about 50 g out of the shell, and about 3 tablespoons beaten. That gives you two ways to measure a fraction of an egg. By volume: beat one egg in a small bowl and use half of it, about 1 1/2 tablespoons. By weight: put the bowl on a scale and use 25 g. The scale is more exact, and it is the method I use for baking, where eggs do structural work and a wrong amount shows up in the texture.

Scaling up is easy. Eggs double and triple cleanly: 2 become 4, 3 become 6, 4 become 12 at a factor of 3. At larger counts, weighing is easier than counting twice. A dozen eggs is about 600 g out of the shell, which is one number on a scale instead of twelve cracks into a bowl. The scaler above rounds counts to whole numbers, so it never asks you for 5.5 eggs.

When the scaled count is not whole, the rounding depends on the bake. For cakes and quick breads, rounding up by half an egg rarely hurts: the extra moisture is forgiving. For cookies and scones, round down, because extra egg makes them spread and go cakey. When in doubt, beat the egg and measure the half. It is ten seconds of work for a result you can trust.

Eggs also set the limit on how far a recipe scales down. A recipe that needs 1 egg cannot be quartered into a quarter of an egg and still work as a bake, because the egg is doing too much of the structure. At that point, the honest answer is to make the full batch and store the extra. A cake keeps well wrapped in the fridge for a few days, and slices freeze beautifully.
